Even in deep-blue California, where registered Democrats outnumber Republicans by nearly two to one, voters proved unwilling to embrace one of the left’s most ambitious taxation experiments. The result also exposed a major divide within the Democratic Party, with Governor Gavin Newsom opposing the proposal over concerns that it could drive entrepreneurs, investors, and businesses out of the state.
California Rejects a $100 Billion Tax Experiment.
Proposition 40 would have targeted Californians with a net worth exceeding $1 billion, taxing assets including stocks, bonds, and privately held businesses. Supporters estimated the measure would generate approximately $100 billion, with 90 percent directed toward healthcare and the remainder funding education and food assistance.
The initiative was promoted as a response to federal healthcare spending reductions enacted under President Donald J. Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Sanders and Democrat Representative Ro Khanna (D-PA) championed the proposal, arguing that wealthier Americans should contribute more toward public services.
However, opponents warned that taxing accumulated wealth rather than realized income could create serious problems for entrepreneurs whose fortunes are tied up in businesses and investments.
Newsom Breaks With the Progressive Left.
Gavin Newsom, the Democrat state governor who is widely considered a potential presidential contender in 2028, warned that the tax could undermine California’s economic competitiveness by encouraging wealthy residents to relocate.
Google co-founders Sergey Brin and Larry Page were among the billionaires who began moving away from California amid the tax controversy. The campaign against Proposition 40 also attracted extraordinary financial support.
Brin and at least 11 other billionaires contributed a combined $269 million to a political committee that spent more than $300 million opposing the measure. Democrat-aligned organizations, including the California Teachers Association and Planned Parenthood’s California affiliates, also opposed the proposal.
Democratic Voters Draw a Fiscal Line.
California voters have rejected Proposition 40 by approximately 53 percent to 47 percent, according to election projections. Concerns about California’s high cost of living, the possibility of wealthy residents fleeing, and the state’s dependence on high-income taxpayers may have contributed to the defeat.
Still, the vote may not be the end of the lefts’ strategy to “tax the rich.” A pre-election survey found more Californians supported higher taxes on billionaires in principle than prioritized retaining wealthy residents, even as support for Proposition 40 itself weakened.
Washington Democrats Face the Same Battle.
The California defeat arrives as Democrats prepare to assume control of Congress, potentially setting the stage for a national confrontation over wealth taxation. Incoming Senate Finance Committee Chairman Ron Wyden has pledged to intensify efforts to tax billionaires, while Sanders and Khanna have also advocated a federal wealth tax.
California’s election shows resistance to such a policy in one of the most deeply blue states, but that does not mean other states across America will reject it. California has the most billionaires in the United States and stands to lose more from them leaving, while other states have far fewer and theoretically risk less.
Though Democrats may have won the political battle against the GOP in November, their most ambitious economic proposals remain far from universally popular.

sources.news_title: Billionaire tax measure on California ballot defeated
California Voters Reject Prop. 40 Billionaire Tax
sources.text:
Noozhawk republishes news articles from CalMatters on state and local policy issues that affect Santa Barbara County readers.
California will not become the first state to levy a wealth tax on its richest residents — at least not this election.
Voters rejected Proposition 40, a proposal to tax billionaires based on their net worth and financial holdings, by 52.8% to 47.2%, according to The Associated Press Monday. The measure had trailed behind for days before The Associated Press confirmed results.
Leaders for Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union pushing the measure, seemed to concede the race minutes before the polls closed but vowed to try again in 2028 if California’s Legislature “fails to deliver a real solution” to fund healthcare hammered by recent federal law.
“That’s not a hypothetical. That’s our plan,” said Dave Regan, president of SEIU-UHW.
Election Day was projected to be an all-around defeat for the union, known for aggressively pursuing ballot measures. Voters defeated union-backed Proposition 44, an effort to control how clinics spend money. Proposition 42, a billionaire tax countermeasure prohibiting future wealth taxes, was leading Monday evening by 51.6% to 48.4%. That measure could get in the way of SEIU-UHW’s future plans to try taxing wealth again.
The billionaire tax would have generated $100 billion for healthcare and education through a one-time, 5% tax on billionaires, according to SEIU-UHW. Opponents of the measure celebrated its defeat.
“Proposition 40 was a reckless experiment conducted on our state’s economy with little regard for the harms it would cause,” according to a statement from Evan Westrop, a campaign strategist for No on Prop. 40.
The opposition campaign, which was backed by wealthy tech investors and healthcare organizations, argued the measure had already driven billionaires from the state and permanently harmed income tax revenue. On Monday they said the state still faces “enormous pressure” to find other ways to fund healthcare hit by federal cuts.
Billionaire Tax Divided Democrats
From the outset, Prop. 40 revealed divisions among the Democratic Party and galvanized some of Silicon Valley’s wealthiest executives to spend hundreds of millions to defeat it.
Gov. Gavin Newsom became one of its earliest opponents, attempting through backroom negotiations to keep it off of the ballot altogether. He endorsed the billionaire-backed counter measure, Prop. 42, designed to ban all wealth taxes in California and kill Prop. 40. Newsom, along with Democratic allies such as Planned Parenthood of California and California Teachers Association, argued a one-time tax would not solve the state’s fiscal woes and would drive wealthy residents out of state.
The California Democratic Party and California Federation of Labor Unions supported the initiative and opposed its counter measures, arguing the state needed more revenue to shield workers and everyday Californians from the effects of dramatic federal healthcare cuts expected to kick 2 million residents off of health insurance.
Lorena Gonzalez, former Assemblymember and president of the California Federation of Labor Unions, said Prop. 40’s failure puts even more pressure on state and federal lawmakers to backfill federal Medicaid cuts.
Supporters of Prop. 40 blamed its loss on billionaires vastly outspending the Yes campaign, which raised $33.5 million.
“That is incredibly corrosive and corrupting to our democracy and our political system, and that’s been dominating the discussion here in California,” Regan said.
Billionaires poured hundreds of millions of dollars into the campaign to stop Prop. 40. Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the charge, publicly moving out of state and donating $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he founded to oppose the tax. The group has served as a passthrough for other billionaire donors to oppose Prop. 40, including by funding the counterpropositions 41 and 42. Collectively, ultra-wealthy opponents donated $378.4 million to oppose the billionaire tax.
In a statement, Abby Lunardini, a spokesperson for Building a Better California, said the billionaire tax threatened to limit revenue for all services in California, including healthcare, by driving economic interests out of the state.
“It was a lose-lose for California, and voters clearly agreed,” Lunardini said.
Ultimately, opponents’ efforts succeeded.
Polling just ahead of the election indicated falling support for Prop. 40 despite growing sentiment for taxing billionaires more in general. According to a UC Berkeley Citrin-POLITICO poll, 45% of voters believed in taxing billionaires more to fund public services compared to 35% who believed the state should prioritize keeping billionaires in state because of the tax revenue and jobs they generate — but just 46% favored Prop. 40.
Infighting among Democrats could have also contributed to Prop. 40’s demise, said John Matsusaka, an economist and direct democracy expert at USC, ahead of the election. Research shows money doesn’t buy people’s votes or values on core issues like abortion, Matsusaka said, but it can exploit uncertainty.
“People these days are very tribal. When your tribe is arguing, people start to listen to the counterarguments,” Matsusaka said.
This article was originally published on CalMatters.

sources.news_title: California Voters Reject 5% Billionaire Wealth Tax Despite Massive Campaign Spending and Democrat Support
sources.text:
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
SACRAMENTO, Calif. — California voters rejected a proposed 5% tax on billionaires’ net worth in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, delivering a defeat to supporters of higher taxes on the wealthy following one of the most expensive ballot measure campaigns in state history.
The Associated Press called the race Monday evening, Nov. 9, determining that Proposition 40 had failed after several days of ballot counting. The measure was losing by approximately 52.8% to 47.2% when the outcome was projected.
Proposition 40 would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on California residents and qualifying trusts with net assets exceeding $1 billion, making it the first state-level wealth tax of its kind in the United States.
Supporters estimated the measure would generate approximately $100 billion over five years, primarily to offset reductions in federal health care funding. Opponents warned that taxing accumulated wealth rather than annual income could drive wealthy residents and businesses out of California, ultimately reducing tax revenue and investment.
The proposal was spearheaded by Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, which argued that additional revenue was necessary to protect hospitals, health insurance coverage and public services affected by federal spending reductions.
Under the measure, 90% of the revenue would have supported health care programs, while the remaining 10% would have funded education and food assistance.
The campaign exposed divisions within California’s Democratic Party.
Outgoing Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom opposed Proposition 40, arguing that the measure could damage the state’s economy by encouraging wealthy entrepreneurs to relocate.
Newsom’s position placed him at odds with U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., and the California Democratic Party, which supported the tax.
Sanders campaigned for the measure during its final weeks, arguing that billionaires should contribute more toward public programs.
However, several organizations traditionally aligned with Democrats joined Newsom in opposing the proposal, including the California Teachers Association, the California Medical Association and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California.
Their opposition reflected concerns about the economic consequences of imposing a wealth tax on a relatively small group of taxpayers who contribute substantial amounts of revenue through existing state income taxes.
The measure also generated significant opposition from Silicon Valley executives.
According to CalMatters’ examination of campaign financing, wealthy opponents contributed approximately $378 million to defeat Proposition 40, compared with roughly $33.5 million raised by its supporters.
Google co-founder Sergey Brin contributed approximately $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee established to oppose the measure.
That committee raised more than $333 million, with Brin accounting for nearly one-third of its funding.
Other technology investors and business executives also contributed to efforts opposing the tax.
The opposition campaign argued that the proposal could weaken California’s technology industry by discouraging investment and encouraging entrepreneurs to establish residency elsewhere.
Brin and fellow Google co-founder Larry Page were among the prominent billionaires reported to have begun moving assets or changing their residency arrangements before the election.
Opponents maintained that the measure could generate substantial revenue initially while undermining California’s long-term tax base.
Supporters disputed those arguments, contending that wealthy residents could afford the proposed assessment without substantially affecting economic activity.
The campaign also highlighted disagreements over how the tax would apply to assets such as corporate stock, private business ownership and other investments.
Unlike income taxes, which generally apply to earnings or realized capital gains, the proposed wealth tax would have been calculated using an assessment of net assets.
Critics argued that valuing privately held businesses and illiquid investments could create administrative and legal complications.
The measure’s opponents also warned that some taxpayers might be required to sell company shares or other assets to satisfy their obligations.
Supporters maintained that the tax was necessary because billionaires can accumulate substantial wealth through appreciating investments without immediately incurring income taxes on those gains.
The election results revealed significant differences among California voters.
According to The Associated Press’ analysis of the ballot measure, most voters younger than 30 supported Proposition 40, while approximately seven in 10 voters age 65 and older opposed it.
Income also influenced voting preferences.
About half of voters with annual household incomes below $100,000 supported the measure, while approximately six in 10 voters earning $100,000 or more opposed it.
Geographically, the proposal received stronger support in liberal urban areas, including San Francisco and Los Angeles, while voters in Orange County and many other parts of the state rejected it.
San Francisco voters supported the proposal by approximately 56% to 44%, according to local election returns.
Despite those pockets of support, the measure failed statewide.
The defeat comes as California faces uncertainty over future federal health care funding.
SEIU-UHW estimated that the state could lose approximately $100 billion in federal health care support over five years because of spending changes enacted under President Donald Trump’s administration.
The union argued that Proposition 40 would have helped preserve services for low-income residents and patients receiving government-supported medical care.
Following the election, supporters criticized the financial advantages enjoyed by the opposition campaign.
“Buying an election is not the same as winning the debate,” the Yes on 40 campaign said in a statement reported by the Associated Press.
“The billionaires may have bought themselves a temporary victory at the ballot box, but they have not bought themselves an end to this debate, and this is only round one.”
SEIU-UHW President Dave Regan indicated that the organization intends to pursue another billionaire tax proposal in 2028 if lawmakers fail to develop an alternative solution for health care funding.
“That’s not a hypothetical. That’s our plan,” Regan said.
The failed initiative was accompanied by competing measures intended to limit or prohibit future wealth taxes.
Proposition 41, which would have nullified Proposition 40 under certain circumstances, was also defeated.
Another competing measure, Proposition 42, sought to prohibit future state wealth taxes, raising questions about whether supporters could pursue a similar initiative in subsequent elections.
The political debate is also continuing at the federal level.
Sanders and Khanna have advocated federal legislation that would impose a wealth tax on American billionaires, arguing that revenue could support social programs and reduce economic inequality.
Such legislation would face significant legal and political questions, including constitutional challenges over the federal government’s authority to tax unrealized wealth.
For California, the defeat of Proposition 40 leaves existing state tax policies unchanged while preserving debate over how to finance health care and other government programs.
The result also represents a political victory for Newsom and other Democratic leaders who argued that increasing taxes on the state’s wealthiest residents could create long-term economic risks.
The Los Angeles Times reported Monday that approximately 53% of voters opposed the measure despite broader Democratic successes in the midterm elections.
The rejection demonstrates that California voters differentiated between their support for Democratic candidates and their views on a proposed tax targeting billionaires’ accumulated wealth.
Although supporters have pledged to renew the effort, Proposition 40’s defeat prevents California from implementing the proposed 5% wealth tax and leaves future changes to the state’s tax structure dependent on new legislation or another voter-approved initiative.

California voters reject one-time wealth tax on billionaires
By Katie Dolan and Kaanita Iyer, CNN
(CNN) — Voters in California have rejected a measure to impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on residents with a net worth of over $1 billion.
Proposition 40 became one of the highest-profile and expensive fights over ballot measures this election cycle. With the backing of billionaire funders, groups opposing the proposition spent tens of millions of dollars in ads against the measure.
The wealth tax would have applied to around 250 billionaires in California, with the funding raised primarily earmarked for healthcare following federal cuts to Medicaid and other programs.
Tech and corporate leaders had threatened to move their residences, and even their businesses, out of California if the measure passed – potentially depriving the state of crucial jobs. The battle over Proposition 40 was one of the most expensive political fights in the country with Google co-founder Sergey Brin funneling just over $100 million to a group trying to defeat the tax.
California’s Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom had said he would vote against the measure, instead proposing a national tax on billionaires as he eyes a potential 2028 presidential run. Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra, another Democrat, also expressed opposition.
But the measure had the backing of other prominent Democrats, including progressive Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Rep. Ro Khanna of California, along with several unions.
Proponents have said the measure was a necessary response to federal healthcare spending cuts from Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act, estimating a shortfall of about $20 billion per year for California moving forward, which threatens the state’s Medi-Cal program that provides healthcare to low-income Californians. They estimated the wealth tax could raise $100 billion, enough to cover the shortfall for about five years.
Meanwhile, opponents of the measure had argued it could harm the state where they built their businesses and fortunes, with Brin — who was born in Moscow — comparing the tax in a rare comment to The New York Times to the society he fled as a child and saying he doesn’t want California to adopt socialism.
Newsom, in making the case for a national tax, had said Prop 40 would not address other state budget needs like housing, childcare or education and disagreed with “a single advocacy organization” writing “the state’s tax code on its own terms.”
Suzanne Jimenez, a sponsor of the measure as part of the group Yes on 40, accused opponents of running a “deeply misleading and corrupt campaign” and criticized the amount of money they poured into it.
“Buying an election is not the same as winning the debate,” Jimenez said in a statement, adding, “The billionaires may have bought themselves a temporary victory at the ballot box, but they have not bought themselves an end to this debate, and this is only round one. This fight to save patient lives and ensure billionaires pay their fair share has only just begun.”

sources.news_title: Oligarchs got crushed on Election Day, but still managed to kill California's wealth tax dreams
sources.text:
America’s oligarchs fared badly overall on Election Day, but they dodged a bullet in California, and perhaps then some.
California’s Prop. 40, the Billionaire Tax initiative, would have been the nation’s first-ever tax on excessive wealth, a concept Americans have supported in poll after poll. Despite its flaws, the measure would have broken the glass. It would have showed that curbing excessive fortunes is possible in an America whose wealth distribution has grown so skewed that it now resembles that of a kleptocratic developing nation.
But some of the state’s billionaires had other plans. After a healthcare workers union sponsored Prop. 40, they put up more than $330 million to create an advocacy group that would plant doubts and fears in voters’ minds, with an assist from prominent Democrats, most notably Gov. Gavin Newsom.
The billionaire opposition effort not only doomed Prop. 40, but may have convinced voters to pass Prop. 42—one of two competing measures they sponsored—which bars the state from enacting future taxes on many types of wealth. On Monday night, with 83 percent of the votes counted, AP called Prop. 40’s defeat. It has not yet made the call on Prop. 42, which remained ahead by 3.2 percentage points.
Prop. 40 was imperfect. The threat of state tax authorities coming for people’s retirement savings proved powerful, though. sources.news_title: California's proposed 'billionaire tax' fails to pass
sources.text:
California voters have rejected Proposition 40, the state’s proposed one-time tax on billionaires, the Associated Press reported Monday. The measure failed after an expensive campaign that pitted labor unions against some of tech’s wealthiest figures. It was also opposed by Gov. Gavin Newsom.
Nic Carter lives about as far from Silicon Valley as you can get within the continental U.S. but his feelings about California’s proposed tax on billionaires couldn’t have been stronger.
Carter, a Floridian, and a general partner at the crypto-focused venture capital firm Castle Island Ventures, told TechCrunch before the vote that he thought the proposal — it was on the ballot during California’s midterm election last week — would actually have been a huge win for more fiscally conservative states like his own.
“I think it would be great for Florida and Texas if these kinds of taxes pass,” Carter said last week. “I think it’s a shame, frankly, that California has this sort of semi-monopoly on capital formation, and that it’s being squandered by local governance that’s super dysfunctional.”
Proposition 40, otherwise known as the California “billionaire’s tax,” was a ballot measure that proposed the creation of a special one-time 5% wealth tax to be levied against state residents with a net worth of more than $1 billion. The tax, which would have been applied retroactively to anyone who was residing in California on January 1, 2026, would have been used to fund a number of public programs — most notably Medi-Cal, the state’s Medicaid program that provides healthcare to qualifying low-income residents.
Proponents of the proposal — largely labor unions — said it would have inconvenienced a tiny number of state residents, as California has a little over 200 billionaires who own a cumulative total of approximately $2 trillion in wealth. In return, they said, it would generate massive amounts of revenue. Its backers projected it could have raised as much as $100 billion over five years, the likes of which could then have been used to support public healthcare and education.
But opponents argued that it would scare California’s wealthiest residents out of the state and ultimately disincentivize growth. The capital flight argument — that California’s upper crust would permanently flee, thus draining a more consistent source of revenue for the state — dominated conversations online among business leaders in the run-up to the vote. A critical but contested analysis published before the vote claimed the proposal would actually have lost the state money over time.
Carter, who subscribes to this argument, had called the tax a “sword of Damocles hanging” over the heads of founders. The threat, he said, wasn’t just from this particular wealth tax but also from anticipated future taxes.
“You’re signaling to the entrepreneur class that you consider them a resource to be plundered,” he said.
Carter, who frequently works in San Francisco with tech startups, claimed such a tax would “inhibit venture capital investment” because VCs “wouldn’t necessarily want to invest in a company if they knew the founder was going to have to liquidate a huge percentage of their shares.” The logic: Since many billionaires keep a majority of their wealth tied to their companies, it would be inconvenient for newly minted billionaires to make liquid a certain percentage of that wealth just so that they could pay the tax.
Jesse Tinsley, a California entrepreneur who has spent his life working in startups, agreed. Tinsley is the co-founder and CEO of Mainstreet, a fintech holding company that owns employment sites like Employer.com and Recruiter.com. Tinsley founded his first startup many years ago and said that, based on his own experience, what he had accomplished wouldn’t have been possible with the proposed tax. Additionally, he reiterated a widely held fear — that founders, who could be taxed on their corporate assets, would be incentivized to give up control over their companies.
“I bootstrapped my business. I have super voting shares, and I came from a [background as a] college dropout [and] broke firefighter with bad credit and whatnot, and built a business that’s valued into the billions,” Tinsley said last week. “I think [the tax] removes the ability to do something like that.”
Tinsley said he felt the proposed tax “forces founders to opt into a system” where “anyone who wants to become an entrepreneur has to … raise money or some type of capital, or move. Those are basically the only two options.”
One of the key architects of the tax policy, Emmanuel Saez, told TechCrunch before the vote that fears about loss of founder control were unfounded, and not part of the design of the proposal. Saez, a French economics professor at UC Berkeley, helped to create and promote the ballot measure alongside Gabriel Zucman, another Berkeley economist.
“The wealth tax hits you by diluting your economic ownership but [shares] can be easily structured to avoid losing any control rights,” Saez said, pointing to the fact that many billionaires only own a small percent of their companies. He’s also argued that stock can be structured to divorce economic ownership and voting control. Indeed, a common strategy to achieve this is called a dual-class share structure, which gives founders powerful voting rights even with limited shares.
Saez noted that AI has helped to drive a huge explosion in wealth in California but that much of that wealth is tied to a very small number of companies and individuals, many of whom won’t pay much back into the state’s coffers. He pointed out that California doesn’t really generate that much revenue from the billionaire class anyway. The state is estimated to take in about $3 billion a year from this group, representing about 1% of the total amount of revenue brought in between 2025 and 2026.
Despite its populist appeal, Proposition 40 struggled to win over enough Californians and was ultimately rejected. Invariably, many will cite voters’ lack of enthusiasm on a massive influx of spending that the bill’s opponents leveraged. The spending included as much as $379 million from the coffers of billionaires like Google co-founder Sergey Brin, who funneled their money into a multi-pronged media assault designed to discredit it. The AP reported that the “no” side raised roughly 10 times as much as the “yes” side.
Supporters of the measure signaled the fight isn’t over, though. The AP reported that backers said they could put a similar tax back on the ballot in 2028.

sources.news_title: California Voters Reject Billionaire Tax, Exposing Democratic Divide
sources.text:
California voters have rejected Proposition 40, which would have made the state the first in the nation to tax billionaires on their net worth. The Associated Press called the race Monday, six days after Election Day.
The defeat capped a fight that split Democrats at the top. California Governor Gavin Newsom, who is considering a run for president in 2028, opposed the tax, warning it would drive the state’s wealthiest residents away. Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Ro Khanna, two leading progressive lawmakers, championed it.
In the Secretary of State's semi-official count as of 5:14 p.m. Monday, 5,789,026 voters (52.9 percent) had rejected the measure and 5,159,356 (47.1 percent) had supported it.
Read More on News
Opponents outraised supporters about tenfold. Building a Better California, the committee that led the opposition, raised more than $333 million, and Google co-founder Sergey Brin alone gave more than $100 million.
What Voters Rejected
The measure would have charged billionaires who lived in California on January 1, 2026, a one-time tax of 5 percent of their net worth, due in 2027, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office analysis in the official voter guide. Ninety percent of the money would have gone to health care, and the rest to education, food assistance and the cost of running the tax.
The sponsoring union, SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, projected about $100 billion. The analyst's office estimated "tens of billions of dollars spread over several years," along with a "possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year" in state income tax collected from billionaires.
Economists disagreed sharply about whether the state would come out ahead. A Hoover Institution paper estimated the tax would raise about $30 billion, less than a third of the union's projection, partly because nearly 30 percent of the tax base had already left the state. Counting income tax lost as billionaires leave, it put the measure's net value to the state at negative $38.9 billion.
The measure's drafters argued the opposite. A National Bureau of Economic Research paper, co-written by one of them, estimated the tax could raise about $100 billion. It found that California's billionaires pay about 0.2 percent of their wealth a year in state income tax. That comes to about $3.2 billion, or 2.4 percent of the state's income tax revenue.
Money, Countermeasures and Departures
Building a Better California also backed Propositions 41 and 42. Both were written to conflict with the wealth tax. The analyst's office warned that if either got more "yes" votes than Proposition 40, courts could block the billionaire tax even if a majority approved it.
The countermeasures turned out not to be needed to stop the tax, but Proposition 42 may outlast the fight. It would write a ban on new taxes on financial assets, and on most retroactive taxes, into the state constitution. In the Secretary of State's count as of 5:14 p.m. Monday, it was leading 51.7 percent to 48.3 percent, with 5,612,642 votes in favor and 5,244,738 against. AP had not called the measure. It drew about 450,000 more "yes" votes than the billionaire tax did.
Some of the people the tax targeted were already gone. Brin and fellow Google co-founder Larry Page had started moving away from California before the January 1 residency cutoff.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg took a different route. In October filings, Meta disclosed a deal in which he committed to stay in California for eight years, barring "material unforeseen circumstances." In exchange, he receives non-voting shares he can sell to cover a tax bill without losing control of the company.
A Democratic Split
Sanders endorsed the tax in a December 2025 statement he posted on X: "Our nation will not thrive when so few own so much." Khanna, whose district includes much of Silicon Valley, called Proposition 40 "the most important ballot initiative in America" in an October post on X.
Newsom has instead called for a federal minimum tax on the very wealthy, starting at $100 million in net worth. He called Sanders’ focus on inequality “spot-on” but said “on this issue, we fundamentally disagree.”
Polls showed a close race before Election Day. Newsweek reported in October that a UC Berkeley poll found 45 percent of registered voters supported the measure, 43 percent opposed it and 12 percent were undecided.
What Comes Next
If Proposition 42 passes, any future wealth tax would first require voters to amend the state constitution again.
Labor leaders cast the campaign as a first step. As ballots were being counted, California Federation of Labor Unions President Lorena Gonzalez said it was “showing other states that you can look them in the eye.”
Counting continues, and results are not yet certified.
Newsweek reached out to Building a Better California, SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West and Newsom’s office for comment by email Monday night.

Indeed, so far, at least seven billionaires, including film director Steven Spielberg, Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, and PayPal co-founder Peter Thiel, have left California.

Proponents also argue that billionaires can accumulate substantial wealth from the stock market and business valuations without paying income tax on those gains until they are realized. They also contend that those who have benefited the most from the state's robust economy should contribute more toward public services.
The measure created a divide among politicians and organizations that ordinarily align with Democratic priorities. While it was supported by the California Democratic Party and labor unions including SEIU Healthcare Workers West, the principal sponsor of the measure, it was opposed by Gov. Gavin Newsom, former Orange County Rep. Katie Porter, and major healthcare and professional organizations such as the California Medical Association and California Teachers Association.

California Prop. 40 fails: Voters reject one-time 5% wealth tax on billionaires
California voters have rejected a first-in-the-nation tax on the net worth of billionaires following a contentious ballot fight that generated huge spending by some prominent tech leaders eager to stop their taxes from going up.
The measure’s failure is a win for Democratic leaders who opposed it, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, who may run for president in 2028. Critics of the tax, known as Proposition 40, said it would have prompted ultrawealthy taxpayers to leave the state.
Most Californians vote by mail, and any ballot postmarked by Election Day that arrives within a week is counted, meaning it often takes days or even weeks for close races to be settled. The Associated Press determined Monday that ‘no’ had received enough votes to win.
The "no" side raised roughly 10 times as much as the "yes" side. Google co-founder Sergey Brin alone dumped more than $100 million into a political action committee working to defeat the measure.
The measure would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of Californians whose net worth exceeds $1 billion. Most of the money would have been used to backfill federal funding cuts to healthcare, and 10% would have gone toward education and food-assistance programs. SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, which backed the tax, said it was necessary to replace an estimated $100 billion the state will lose in federal healthcare funding over five years.
Proposition 40 was the nation’s biggest test yet on an idea progressives have long championed: raising taxes on the ultra-rich by targeting the main way they make their money — through their investments as opposed to the paychecks they receive from work.
The measure attracted support from liberal leaders beyond the state, including Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, who rallied in cities across California in the race’s closing weeks to urge voters to pass it. The "Yes on 40" campaign did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment.
Billionaires donated millions of dollars to a political action committee, Building a Better California, working to defeat the measure. The committee, which backed other measures on the ballot designed to nullify the tax, raised more than $333 million, nearly a third of which came from Brin.
The AP Voter Poll indicates that the majority of young voters in California — those younger than 30 — voted "yes" on Proposition 40. Older voters were far less supportive, with roughly 7 in 10 voters who were 65 and older saying they voted "no" on the ballot measure.
About half of voters with a household income under $100,000 annually said they were in support of the initiative. Closer to 6 in 10 California voters with an income of $100,000 or higher said they were opposed.
Brin, along with his fellow Google co-founder Larry Page, was among the billionaires who started cutting ties with the state in anticipation of the possible tax. Another tech mogul, Mark Zuckerberg, said he would remain in the state for eight years and made a deal with Meta to help him pay the tax without losing his ownership stake in the company.
Some traditional Democratic allies, including Planned Parenthood and the California Medical Association, were part of a coalition opposing it. They were concerned about how the tax revenue would be divvied up and about the potential impact on the state’s budget if there was a mass exodus of wealthy taxpayers. California’s budget relies heavily on the income tax of the state’s richest residents.
"Proposition 40 was a reckless experiment conducted on our state’s economy with little regard for the harms it would cause," the coalition said in a statement.
Robert Swonger, an auto glass technician living near Sacramento who’s politically independent, said before voting concluded Nov. 3 that he planned to vote against it.
"Obviously, I would like billionaires not to have as much money as they do," he said. "But I don’t believe taxing them out of existence is going to work."
Progressive politicians, including Sanders and Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, have long supported a federal wealth tax. Newsom says a California wealth tax would disadvantage the state, but he supports a national minimum tax on anyone with a net worth above $100 million.
Days before Sanders held rallies in California cities last month, Newsom told reporters that the senator’s focus on wealth inequality was "spot-on." But he said that "on this issue, we fundamentally disagree."
Supporters of the California tax started running ads recently in New Hampshire, New Mexico and Virginia, states that will vote early in the Democratic presidential primary in 2028, that criticize Newsom for his opposition to the measure.
The Source: This Associated Press report referenced AP's Voter Poll findings, campaign fundraising figures, and statements from supporters and opponents of the measure.

Prop. 40 sought to require individuals or couples whose net worth exceeded $1 billion as of Dec. 31, 2026, to pay a one-time tax equal to 5% of their wealth.

sources.news_title: Silicon Valley's billionaires won the tax battle. The war on wealth is just beginning.
sources.text:
For many in the tech industry, the midterms landed like a hangover after a two-year bender. In the sober light of day, their flirtations with MAGA and extravagant spending may now seem embarrassing. Yet for Silicon Valley's billionaire class, there's still reason to keep the champagne flowing after the election — because it still pays to be rich.
California voters have rejected prop 40, a landmark initiative to impose a one-time 5% tax on billionaires in the state. They also seem to favor a countermeasure, prop 42, that would hamstring any future attempts to tax financial assets —the kind that separate the rich from the really rich. (Votes are still being tallied.) That people in the most progressive state with the highest wealth inequality in the country made such decisions in the bluest national election in recent history is either a failure of populism, or a victory of free enterprise, depending on who you ask. On X, Mike Solana of Peter Thiel's Founders Fund heralded Prop 40's apparent defeat succinctly: "Eat shit, communists."
More than 200 billionaires live in California. Cumulatively, they hold an estimated $2.3 trillion in wealth, a sum that UC Berkeley economist Gabriel Zucman notes is roughly equivalent to the combined annual income of every single resident in the state. Soon, there could be dozens more, as companies like Anthropic and OpenAI prepare world-historic IPOs. (Anthropic's alone could mint close to a thousand centimillionaires.) Wealth for these people is not a matter of salary, but of assets. Most fortunes in the tech industry remain in company equity, which is untaxed until shares are sold. That has allowed some of the richest people in the state to avoid paying much in income tax: Billionaires like Mark Zuckerberg, Larry Ellison, and Larry Page all famously take $1 salaries.
"The way this system works is they can literally create gigantic fortunes without paying tax," says Tom Steyer, an investor and former gubernatorial candidate, and one of the few billionaires to come out in support of the billionaire tax. "We know where we need to go, which is a fairer tax system."
Prop 40 offered one such alternative. Supporters argued that it would mark a long overdue correction, and still allow billionaires to remain very, very rich. "The poorest billionaire in California will make about $300 million this year. If we pass the CA wealth tax, he will only make $235 million," Saikat Chakrabarti, a former Stripe engineer and political adviser, wrote on X. Critics argued that asking billionaires to pay cash on their paper wealth would ruin the tech economy, forcing them to sell off parts of private companies, and inspiring an exodus from the state. Earlier this year, the investor Balaji Srinivasan noted on X that Larry Page, Sergey Brin, Elon Musk, and Peter Thiel had already "exited the failed state of California," and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan warned that should a billionaire tax pass, many startup founders would choose not to come to California at all.
If prop 40 is "not the way to skin the cat, don't come back and tell me there's no way to skin the cat," says Tom Steyer.
The would-be victims of the billionaire tax feared those outcomes enough to form a coalition, which included prominent names in tech — Brin, Patrick Collison, Eric Schmidt, and John Doerr among them. Together, they spent more than $300 million to defeat the measure (including a reported $148 million ad campaign), the most ever spent by one side on a single ballot initiative. Supporters, by comparison, spent about $2 million on ads. "The disparity in money in this thing was too high," says Cooper Teboe, a political strategist in Silicon Valley. "There was a genuine marketing gap."
Money isn't everything. In Texas, where sometimes trillionaire Elon Musk spent nearly $500 million trying to keep Republicans in office, voters turned around and elected a Democratic governor for the first time since 1991, and a Democratic Senator who made reining in data centers a major part of his message. Both of those campaigns were modeled on the idea of a "top versus bottom" rather than "left versus right" politics — that is, an alignment over class interests above all else.
The zealous interest from both sides of prop 40 — and the fact that some 46% of voters in California favored the tax despite what many saw as significant flaws — are signs that conversations about wealth taxation are just getting started. Most Americans think billionaires don't pay enough in taxes, according to a national survey from last year; one study found that 73% of Americans would favor a "special additional tax on billionaires." In April, a Pew survey found that 60% of people believed that corporations and very wealthy people did not pay "their fair share" in taxes.
That's led some proponents of a wealth tax to shift their gaze nationally. Indeed, some of prop 40's detractors, including Governor Gavin Newsom, made the argument that they would rather tax wealth federally than on the state level. Other opponents, who had grievances with the details of prop 40 — like what its actual fiscal impact would be, how the state would assess wealth, and where all of that hypothetical money would actually go — have come out in support of wealth taxes in general. Steyer, who supports the idea of a federal tax on billionaires, says that if prop 40 is "not the way to skin the cat, don't come back and tell me there's no way to skin the cat."
Having a plan for taxing the ultra rich "becomes almost a prerequisite for whoever ends up as the dominant 2028 candidate," says Teboe. "The war continues."

sources.news_title: California Voters Reject Prop 40 Billionaire Tax After Seven Moguls Fled With $540 Billion in Wealth
sources.text:
California Voters Reject Prop 40 Billionaire Tax After Seven Moguls Fled With $540 Billion in Wealth
Stanford study says the levy would have raised just $30 billion, not the $100 billion promised
California's Proposition 40 billionaire tax appears headed for defeat after the 3 November vote, with Stanford researchers estimating that seven wealthy residents had already taken $540 billion (£412 billion) beyond its potential tax base.
Associated Press returns showed about 53% against the measure and 47% in favour, with counting continuing. Supporters had cast the one-time 5% tax as a way to make the ultra-wealthy pay their fair share. It would have funded healthcare, food assistance, and education programmes facing federal cuts. The proposal applied to residents with more than $1 billion (about £750 million) in assets as of the January cutoff.
The Exodus That Came First
Opponents warned for months that billionaires could flee if the tax passed. The sharper point, which rivals largely sidestepped, is that many had already gone. Their early exits became central to the debate.
A working paper by Stanford economists Joshua Rauh and Benjamin Jaros, published through the National Bureau of Economic Research, found that seven billionaires left California before the January 1, 2026 residency cutoff, taking roughly 30% of the state's billionaire wealth out of reach of the tax.
Peter Thiel, Larry Page, and Sergey Brin were among those the researchers identified as having moved. Under their estimates, California arguably risked losing both the revenue and the tax before voters ever marked a ballot.
A Hundred Billion That Was Never There
Supporters, led by the Service Employees International Union's healthcare arm, projected the tax would raise $100 billion (£75 billion) over several years. That projection became a major campaign talking point. The Stanford paper estimated it would have collected closer to $30 billion (£23 billion), less than a third of that, once the early exits were counted. The authors also argued that lost future income-tax revenue from departing billionaires would have left the state worse off overall.
The measure's designers pushed back. Economist Gabriel Zucman, who helped shape the proposal, contended that some high-profile leavers, including Brin, probably remained California tax residents on the cutoff date because of their continuing ties to the state. That dispute over who actually counts as gone sat at the centre of the fight.
What Californians Stand To Lose
The stakes reach past the billionaires. Most of the revenue was meant to shore up the state's healthcare system against federal Medicaid cuts, with the rest going to food aid and schools. The potential shortfall raises difficult questions about funding. Those are services ordinary Californians use, and the budget still leans heavily on a small group of top earners whose income taxes the state cannot easily replace.
Billionaire-backed opponents raised about $389 million (£297 million), with Brin contributing around $102 million. Supporters raised about $33 million (£25 million). The fight was among California's most expensive ballot campaigns. Governor Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, opposed the measure, warning it could drive wealthy residents out.
A Door Closing on Future Attempts
Proposition 42, a billionaire-backed measure that would bar new state taxes on financial assets and other personal property, while blocking most retroactive taxes, was also heading towards approval. Associated Press returns showed about 52% support.
Together, the apparent results hand Silicon Valley a win and could make any future wealth tax far harder to revive.

Voters rejected the “billionaire tax” in California — but approved a variety of other taxes, especially at the local level.
It was a remarkable result in an election in which voters constantly said that the cost of living was the top concern.
California politicians complain about “affordability,” then make the state more unaffordable. And with Democrats, there are almost never any controls on spending, no careful management of funds, no accountability to the taxpayers. Their only solution to every fiscal crunch is: Raise taxes.
And voters seem to have gone along with it.
Here’s just a partial list of local results.
In San Francisco, voters passed Measure H, which creates an annual parcel tax on local property to fund the city’s ailing Muni transport system. Voters in the broader Bay Area also chose to raise sales taxes through Measure RTM to fund BART and other transit agencies.
In San Diego, voters appear to have passed Measure B, which raise county sales taxes by 0.5%, some of which would supposedly go toward health services.
In Los Angeles, voters passed Measure FD, which will raised sales taxes in the city by 0.5% to provide funding to the fire department that the city should arguably be providing already.
That’s on top of the 0.5% sales tax that voters passed in LA County in June, which was sold as a way to pay for local health care services.
Even in formerly conservative Orange County, voters passed sales tax and hotel tax hikes in some towns.
What’s remarkable about these results is that voters weren’t raising taxes on other people, in most cases, but rather on themselves.
It could be that the same “blue wave” that brought left-wing voters to the polls also resulted in more tax hikes.
But that cannot explain the fact that the billionaire tax failed.
Maybe the billionaires who opposed Proposition 40 did a better job of explaining the consequences to voters.
Somehow there is a disconnect in voters’ minds between voting for higher sales taxes on Election Day, and paying more for groceries every other day.
Proponents of local sales tax hikes are good at explaining what the money is for, in theory. Who wouldn’t want the fire department to have more equipment?
But voters rarely hear the other side of the argument: That LA could fund the fire department if it hadn’t wasted billions on homeless services that made no impact whatsoever.
Whatever the reason, California voters need to understand they are making their own lives more expensive.
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association has been a lone voice defending Proposition 13 — which limits property tax hikes — for decades.
It’s time for other California leaders to step up and say: enough.

sources.news_title: California Matters: California’s election featured a big showdown over taxes. Wealth tax defeat was the biggest
sources.text:
California adopted the initiative system — allowing proposed laws to bypass the Legislature and be placed on the ballot via petition — in 1911, but until the 1970s it was scantily used.
Since 1971, no year has passed without at least a few and sometimes dozens of measures being filed, records from the Secretary of State’s office show. The most was in 2005, when 109 ballot proposals were cleared for signature gathering.
Since 1911, a total of 2,194 measures have gained permission to circulate petitions: 410 qualified for the ballot and, not counting this year’s crop, just 141 survived to become law.
Despite the less than 30% rate of success, the initiative process has evolved into a powerful tool for changing governmental policy. Sometimes even the threat to qualify an initiative can force the Legislature to act.
Proposition 13, the iconic 1978 measure to limit property taxes and make enactment of other taxes more difficult, stands as the ultimate example of that power. However, this year’s ballot offered a measure, Proposition 40, that would rival Prop. 13 in impact.
The votes in the Nov. 3 election are still being counted, but Prop. 40, which would impose a 5% tax on the wealth of California’s billionaires, was consistently running behind by roughly 5 percentage points as votes were being tallied last week.
Pre-election polls had indicated Prop. 40, which enjoyed popularity earlier in the year, had dropped into negative territory.
In a sense, its apparent failure should not be surprising.
It was placed on the ballot by the Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West to improve financial support for medical services that faced cuts in both federal and state funds.
The union said the one-time tax could raise as much as $100 billion, but its campaign for the measure was relatively weak, while the billionaires targeted by Prop. 40 pumped several hundred million dollars into a massive media campaign against it.
Prop. 40 also suffered from deep divisions within the Democratic Party and within the labor union community, the latter because most of the revenues would have gone to healthcare, rather than being shared with other services, such as education.
Dave Regan, the pugnacious leader of SEIU-UHW, vowed to try again if the Legislature “fails to deliver a real solution” to healthcare support.
“That’s not a hypothetical. That’s our plan,” Regan said.
The recent election was a double-barreled loss for Regan. By a huge margin, voters also rejected his Proposition 44, which would have required clinics serving low-income patients to spend 90% of their annual revenue on patient care.
Moreover, voters appear to have approved Proposition 42, a measure placed on the ballot by Prop. 40’s wealthy opponents to counter the wealth tax. It places a prohibition of taxing personal wealth into the state constitution.
By prohibiting some taxes, Prop. 42 is, in effect, a win for the state’s tax limitation advocates — the same groups that backed Prop. 13 about 48 years ago and have jousted with unions and other pro-tax forces ever since.
Prop. 42 partially offsets voters’ rejection of Proposition 43, which would have made passage of local government taxes more difficult, and their approval of Proposition 3, which makes a temporary hike in income taxes on high-earning Californians, first approved in 2012, permanent.
Putting all of these issues together, this mid-term election was another in a long string of ballot measure confrontations between pro- and anti-tax advocates — with rejection of Prop. 40, the biggest of the bunch, giving the anti-tax faction a win on points.
Had Prop. 40 passed, it would have, like Prop. 13 in 1978, fueled a national taxation battle. Taxing personal wealth has become a holy grail goal for the Democratic Party’s uber-progressive wing.
Dan Walters is a journalist and author who writes for CALmatters.org, a nonprofit, nonpartisan media venture explaining California policies and politics.

California faces one-two punch as voters reject wealth tax and billionaires eye exits
Voters rejected a proposed one-time tax on billionaire wealth, but the fight over California’s tax climate and the risk of losing wealthy residents is far from over
California voters rejected a proposed one-time 5% tax on billionaire wealth, turning back a measure supporters said could raise tens of billions of dollars for healthcare. The tax would have applied to people who were California residents on Jan. 1, 2026, with payments spread over five years.
The defeat came as some of the state’s wealthiest residents warned they could leave California over the proposal. The state has one of the nation’s largest billionaire populations and relies heavily on high earners to fund its budget, making the potential loss of additional wealthy residents a concern for state finances.
Supporters, including Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and the Service Employees International Union–United Healthcare Workers West, said the tax could help offset Trump administration cuts to healthcare and food assistance. California Gov. Gavin Newsom opposed the tax, arguing that California should address wealth inequality without driving billionaires out of the state.
CALIFORNIA WEALTH TAX PROPOSAL HEMORRHAGES $1T AS BILLIONAIRES FLEE
Voters were also weighing Proposition 42, a separate measure backed by tech billionaires to block new taxes on personal property. It was leading, and approval could make future efforts to tax billionaire wealth harder, though supporters have vowed to keep pushing.
Wayne Winegarden, a senior fellow in business and economics at the Pacific Research Institute, said concerns that the tax could expand beyond billionaires and drive wealthy residents away may have hurt its support.
"A lot of messaging went around this: ‘You’re next.’ And I think that messaging resonated with people. This is most likely not a one-time tax. It’s not going to just stick to billionaires," he said.
CEO SAYS DOING BUSINESS IN STATE ‘SUCKS’ AS COMPANY HEADS TO TEXAS AMID CALIFORNIA EXODUS
Winegarden said voters may also have feared that billionaire departures would leave less money for the state budget.
"People were nervous that you’re going to lose money off of this because of billionaires leaving. The macroeconomic impacts of the wealth tax meant that the rest of the budget was going to have less money. I think that message got out there, and I think that helped," he said.
Winegarden said defeating the tax could halt departures tied to the proposal, but he argued California remains uncompetitive on taxes.
"Without the wealth tax, the continued bleeding from a wealth-tax perspective should stop. Now, California has been, from a tax-competitiveness perspective, very uncompetitive."
RED STATES HAVE SPENT DECADES DOMINATING A KEY CORNER OF THE ECONOMY
His comments point to broader concerns that California’s tax policies could push wealth and investment elsewhere. The state is already losing taxpayers to other states.
Los Angeles County, home to Hollywood and one of the nation’s largest economic engines, led the country in taxpayer losses. A net 17,496 tax filers left for other states, taking nearly $1.9 billion in income with them.
The outflow extended beyond Los Angeles.

With roughly three-quarters of ballots counted, about 54% opposed the measure and 46% supported it. The Associated Press had not yet called the race Friday, but Proposition 40 had consistently trailed by a substantial margin.
The proposal would have applied to roughly 250 California billionaires and generated tens of billions of dollars, according to state estimates. Ninety percent of the revenue would have gone toward healthcare, with the remainder funding food assistance and education programs.
Opponents dramatically outspent supporters. Billionaires and business groups poured more than $300 million into efforts opposing Proposition 40 and promoting competing measures that could have blocked it. Google co-founder Sergey Brin alone contributed more than $100 million.
Gov. Gavin Newsom also opposed the measure, arguing it could encourage wealthy residents to leave California and destabilize state revenues. Supporters, including Sen. Bernie Sanders and the California Democratic Party, argued billionaires should contribute more toward healthcare and social programs.
The defeat does not necessarily end the wealth-tax debate. Democratic leaders nationally have already indicated that taxing extremely wealthy Americans will remain part of their agenda.

sources.news_title: California rejects billionaire tax proposal in win for executives, Newsom
Voters in Silicon Valley rejected the billionaire wealth tax while those in Los Angeles and San Francisco—home to the two top AI companies—wanted it
sources.text:
California is still counting the votes for the 2026 election, but the controversial billionaire wealth tax looks headed for defeat—with help from Silicon Valley.
Statewide, the “no” side for Proposition 40 is getting 55% of the vote versus 45% voting “yes.” That split exactly matches how it played out in Santa Clara County, home to tech strongholds like Sunnyvale, Palo Alto, Cupertino, and Mountain View.
The wealthy Bay Area enclave of Marin County, which sits just north of San Francisco, also came out against Prop 40 as did San Mateo County, which is just south of the city.
By contrast, 55% of San Francisco County voters were in favor of Prop 40 and 45% were against. That’s despite being home to top AI startups OpenAI and Anthropic, which are planning to go public soon and will create new millionaires—and billionaires.
Of course, plenty of employees and early investors in the AI giants live outside San Francisco and likely voted according to their pocketbooks as Prop 40 sought a one-time 5% tax on billionaires.
Opponents of the ballot measure warned it was unlikely to remain a one-time levy, and the way it would’ve taxed privately held assets raised fears founders might have to sell controlling stakes in their companies.
That concern may have resonated especially across the startups and venture capital firms in Silicon Valley who are not quite billionaires yet but have aspirations to become one.
Fearing the possibility of a wealth tax, several billionaires have already fled California, including Google cofounder Sergey Brin, who helped finance the campaign to defeat Prop 40.
And because the state already relies heavily on the wealthy for its budget, it doesn’t take much to move the needle, which perhaps weighed on voters’ minds as well.
The loss of just six billionaires drastically reduced estimates of how much the wealth tax would’ve raised in revenue while also cutting forecasts for how much revenue California could generate from income taxes in the future.
Meanwhile, the election results revealed another split within the state. Los Angeles County voters were in favor of Prop 40, 53% versus 47%.
Unlike Northern California, which is a tech hub that’s leading the AI charge, Southern California is an entertainment hub that’s threatened by AI-generated content.
Alongside the campaign against Prop 40, opponents also pushed competing ballot measures designed to nullify the proposed billionaire wealth tax.
One of them is leading in the vote tally. Prop 42 would prohibit taxes on personal savings, assets and retirement holdings.
It dovetailed with a key anti-Prop 40 message, namely that the billionaire tax could someday be expanded to includes everyone else’s wealth, too.
But Prop 40’s defeat and Prop 42’s ban on future wealth taxes doesn’t mean the issue is going away forever. In fact, even some of the opponents of the billionaire tax were against it because it was restricted to one state and not a nationwide levy that would be harder to dodge.
“A ‘no’ vote doesn’t mean similar measures won’t ever be implemented,” Michael Feispor, partner on EY’s private tax team, said in a statement. “Taxpayers who have been watching from the sidelines should use this window to revisit their residency, domicile, and estate planning structures—because now they have some more time to plan.”
He added that wealthy Californians are already asking hard questions about residency, with some acting on them.
For those who remain in the state, methods for organizing wealth that avoid steep estate taxes, such as irrevocable trusts, are becoming more important.
“The question isn’t whether this kind of tax or something similar comes back—it’s whether taxpayers are prepared when it does,” Feispor said. “Whatever the outcome, this tax debate isn’t over and has elevated the importance of long-term planning for individuals and families.”
